lessons.title: Why water entropy runs the show
lessons.search: hydrophobic effect entropy water cage biochemistry

blocks.p: Here's the one idea this whole unit hangs on: **water wants freedom**. Liquid water is constantly swapping hydrogen-bond partners (the slides call these "flickering clusters"). Every way a water molecule can tumble and re-pair is entropy, and more entropy is favorable.

blocks.h: What a nonpolar molecule does to water

blocks.p: Water can't hydrogen bond to something greasy like isobutane. So the water touching it has fewer ways to arrange itself and gets locked into an ordered **cage** (hydration sphere). Less freedom = **lower entropy of the water**. That's what "solvent structure means less entropy" means.

If two greasy molecules clump together, the total surface touching water shrinks, so fewer water molecules are caged. Those freed waters gain entropy. That entropy gain is what pushes nonpolar things together. It's not that grease loves grease (London dispersion is tiny, about 0.3 kJ/mol). It's that water gets happier when grease hides.

blocks.key: Hydrophobic effect = entropy-driven. Nonpolar groups cluster because it **increases the entropy of water**, not because of strong attractions between the nonpolar groups.

blocks.p: **ΔG = ΔH − TΔS**. Negative ΔG = spontaneous. A big positive ΔS (water freed) makes −TΔS large and negative, so ΔG goes negative even if ΔH barely changes.

list: **Enthalpic effects (ΔH)** = bonds and attractions made or broken: H-bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals.
**Entropic effects (ΔS)** = freedom and disorder: mostly water freedom in this class, plus chain flexibility.

blocks.h: Why salts and polar stuff dissolve

blocks.p: Urea dissolves great because it H-bonds with water, so water can keep moving and swapping partners around it. Salt dissolves because spreading ions out through the solution raises the entropy of the whole solution (that's also where osmotic pressure comes from).

example.q: Two hydrophobic side chains are buried in a protein core. In plain words, what is the main thing driving that burial?
example.a: The water that would have been caged around those side chains gets freed up. Water entropy goes up (ΔS > 0), which makes ΔG negative. The small attraction between the side chains is a minor bonus.

videos.title: The Hydrophobic Effect and Entropy, made super simple

lessons.title: Urea, IPA, and the direct vs indirect models
lessons.search: urea protein denaturation direct indirect mechanism

blocks.p: Denaturants like urea (and alcohols like isopropanol, IPA) unfold proteins. Your review sheet wants you to know **two ways** that could happen, and which one wins.

head: Model
What the denaturant does
Which term
rows: Binds right onto the protein (backbone and side chains) with H-bonds and van der Waals contacts. Unfolded protein exposes more surface to grab, so unfolding is favored.
Messes with water's structure and freedom so that exposing hydrophobic groups costs less entropy. The hydrophobic effect gets weaker, so the core falls apart more easily.

blocks.key: Direct = enthalpic. Indirect = entropic. The **mixed model** best represents what really happens.

blocks.h: Urea vs IPA on water structure

list: **Urea** H-bonds with water really well. Water can still move around it, so it only lowers water's entropy a little. It also H-bonds directly to the protein backbone (direct).

**IPA** has an OH that can H-bond, but also a greasy isopropyl chunk. That greasy part orders water around it (lower water entropy) and can sit right against hydrophobic side chains, which makes burying them less worth it.

blocks.tip: The IPA details weren't in the slide text I had access to. If Dr. Tracy framed IPA differently in class, go with his version. The direct/indirect/mixed framework is the part the review sheet names.

example.q: A student says urea unfolds proteins only because it H-bonds to the peptide backbone. What's missing from that answer?
example.a: That's only the direct (enthalpic) piece. Urea also changes water structure, weakening the entropy-driven hydrophobic effect (indirect). The mixed model, both together, is the best description.

questions.question: What does it mean to say that solvent structure means less entropy?
options: Ordered water around a solute has fewer possible arrangements
Structured water forms more hydrogen bonds, which raises ΔS
Water near a solute moves faster, so its entropy drops
Structured solvent breaks covalent bonds, which lowers ΔS
questions.explanation: When water is forced into an ordered cage it loses ways to arrange itself, so its entropy goes down.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the hydrophobic effect?
options: Nonpolar groups attract each other through strong dispersion forces
Nonpolar groups cluster, freeing caged water and raising its entropy
Nonpolar groups form hydrogen bonds once they are out of the water
Nonpolar groups cluster because it lowers the enthalpy of the water
questions.explanation: Clustering shrinks the caged surface, freeing water molecules. That entropy gain drives it, not strong attractions.

questions.question: For protein folding, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Which change most directly makes folding spontaneous in water?
options: A large decrease in the entropy of the surrounding water
A large increase in the entropy of the surrounding water
A large increase in the entropy of the polypeptide chain
A large positive ΔH from breaking internal hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: Burying hydrophobic residues frees water, so ΔS of the water rises and −TΔS pushes ΔG negative.

questions.question: Why is urea very soluble in water while isobutane is not?
options: Urea H-bonds with water, so water keeps its freedom of motion
Urea is larger, so it fits between water molecules more easily
Isobutane H-bonds too strongly and pulls water out of solution
Isobutane is charged, so water forms a tight shell and precipitates
questions.explanation: Urea H-bonds with water so water can still move and swap partners. Isobutane can't, so water must form an ordered cage.

questions.question: In the direct model of urea denaturation, what drives unfolding?
options: Urea changes water structure so exposed hydrophobic groups cost less
Urea binds the protein directly, an enthalpically favored contact
Urea covalently breaks the peptide bonds in the protein backbone
Urea raises the pH so ionizable side chains lose their charges
questions.explanation: Direct = urea makes favorable contacts (H-bonds, van der Waals) with the protein itself. That's an enthalpic effect.

questions.question: The indirect model of denaturation is mainly which kind of effect?
options: Enthalpic, from new hydrogen bonds between urea and backbone
Entropic, from changing water structure and the hydrophobic effect
Covalent, from urea reducing the disulfide bonds in the protein
Electrostatic, from urea neutralizing charged side chains
questions.explanation: Indirect = the denaturant alters water, weakening the entropy-driven hydrophobic effect. That's entropic.

questions.question: According to the course, which model best represents how urea/IPA denature proteins?
questions.explanation: The mixed model, with both direct (enthalpic) and indirect (entropic) contributions, is the best representation.

questions.question: Salt dissolving in water is favorable mainly because:
options: Spreading the ions out raises the entropy of the whole solution
Ions form covalent bonds with water that release a lot of heat
Water forms rigid cages around ions that lower the enthalpy
Ions lower the temperature, so the −TΔS term gets smaller
questions.explanation: Diluting a solid salt into solution increases entropy of the whole system. Osmotic pressure comes from that same entropy gain.

questions.question: Which interaction is the weakest per contact, even though the hydrophobic effect it's linked to is a major folding force?
options: Covalent C–C bonds in the backbone
questions.explanation: London dispersion forces are tiny (around 0.3 kJ/mol). The hydrophobic effect is strong because of water entropy, not these contacts.

questions.question: Which of these are entropic effects in protein folding or binding? (Select all that apply)
options: Water released from cages when hydrophobic surfaces are buried
Loss of chain flexibility as the polypeptide becomes compact
A new salt bridge forming between Lys and Glu side chains
A hydrogen bond forming between two backbone amide groups
questions.explanation: Water freedom and chain freedom are entropy (ΔS). Salt bridges and H-bonds are bonds, so they're enthalpic (ΔH).

questions.question: A substrate drifts toward an enzyme's hydrophobic pocket before any bonds form. According to the slides, what pushes it there first?
options: The entropy of water around both surfaces
Gravity acting on the heavier substrate
questions.explanation: The first step of binding is the substrate being pushed toward the enzyme by water entropy, the same hydrophobic logic as folding.

questions.question: Which describe isopropanol (IPA) compared to urea? (Select all that apply)
options: IPA has a nonpolar part that orders nearby water
IPA can contact hydrophobic side chains directly
IPA cannot form any hydrogen bonds with water
IPA acts only by breaking covalent peptide bonds
questions.explanation: IPA's OH can H-bond, but its greasy isopropyl group orders water and can sit against hydrophobic side chains, weakening the drive to bury them.

lessons.title: The 20 amino acids, grouped so they stick
lessons.search: memorize 20 amino acids structures one letter code

blocks.p: You have to know all 20 by **name, one-letter code, structure, and group**. Memorizing them in groups is way easier than as a list of 20.

head: Group
Amino acids (code)
What to notice
rows: Gly **G**, Ala **A**, Pro **P**, Val **V**, Leu **L**, Ile **I**, Met **M**
Greasy carbon chains. Gly has just H. Pro's side chain loops back onto its own backbone N (a ring).
Rings. Tyr has an OH. Trp and Tyr absorb light at 280 nm (that's how you measure protein concentration).
OH, SH, or amide groups. Cys can form disulfide bonds.
Amine-type groups that hold a + charge. His pKa ~6, so it flips near body pH.
Extra carboxylic acid. Negative at pH 7.

blocks.h: The one-letter codes that don't match

list: **R** = Arg ("aRginine")
**F** = Phe ("Fenylalanine")
**Y** = Tyr ("tYrosine")
**W** = Trp ("tWo rings")
**K** = Lys (K is next to L in the alphabet)
**D** = Asp ("asparDic")
**E** = Glu ("glutEmic")
**N** = Asn ("asparagiNe")
**Q** = Gln ("Q-tamine")

blocks.tip: The easy-to-mix pairs: Asp D vs Asn N (acid vs amide), Glu E vs Gln Q (acid vs amide), Ser vs Thr (Thr has one extra CH₃), Leu vs Ile (same formula, branch in a different spot).

list: Every amino acid has an amine, a carboxylic acid, and an R group on the α-carbon.
All are chiral **except Gly**, and life uses the **L** form.
Gly and Pro tend to cause kinks and promote non-helical structure.

example.q: Write the sequence Glu-Lys-Trp-Asn-Phe in one-letter code.

videos.title: Memorize and Draw the 20 Amino Acids
Memorize the 20 Amino Acids, the easy way

lessons.title: pKa and charge: the only rule you need
lessons.search: amino acid pKa charge henderson hasselbalch titration curve

blocks.p: pKa is the pH where a group is **half protonated, half not**. Compare the pH to the pKa and you know the charge.

blocks.key: Acids go from 0 to −1. Bases go from +1 to 0. Below the pKa the H⁺ is on; above the pKa it's off.

blocks.h: Numbers worth knowing (exam gives you a table, but know the ballpark)

list: α-carboxyl: about **2** (the course says ~2 to 4)
α-amino: about **9–10** (course says ~9 to 11)

blocks.p: **pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])**. At pH = pKa, the ratio is 1:1. One unit above the pKa, it's 10:1 deprotonated (~91%). Two units above, ~99%. The flat part (plateau) of a titration curve sits at the pKa: that's the buffer region.

example.q: At pH 7, what's the charge on a Lys side chain (pKa 10.5) and an Asp side chain (pKa 3.9)?
example.a: Lys: pH is below its pKa, so it's still protonated, NH₃⁺, **+1**. Asp: pH is above its pKa, so it's deprotonated, COO⁻, **−1**.

example.q: A buffer has 0.2 M acetic acid and 0.2 M acetate, pKa 4.76. pH?

videos.title: Amino acid titration calculation using Henderson–Hasselbalch
Proportion of amino acids (Henderson–Hasselbalch practice)

questions.question: Which one-letter code is correct?
questions.explanation: W is Trp. Lys is K, Gln is Q, Arg is R.

questions.question: Which one-letter code belongs to aspartate?
questions.explanation: Asp = D. Asn = N, Glu = E, Ala = A.

questions.question: Which one-letter code belongs to phenylalanine?
questions.explanation: Phe = F. Pro = P, Tyr = Y, His = H.

questions.question: Which amino acids have side chains that are positively charged at pH 7? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Lys and Arg are + at pH 7. His (pKa ~6) is mostly neutral at 7. Glu is negative; Ser and Asn are uncharged.

questions.question: Which amino acids are aromatic? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Phe, Tyr, and Trp are the aromatic group in Lehninger. (His has a ring but is grouped with the positive amino acids.)

questions.question: Why do proteins absorb light at 280 nm?
options: Aromatic rings in Trp and Tyr
questions.explanation: Trp and Tyr absorb at 280 nm because of their aromatic rings. That's how A = εbc measures protein concentration.

questions.question: Which amino acid is NOT chiral?
questions.explanation: Gly's side chain is just H, so its α-carbon has two identical groups. All others are chiral and L in proteins.

questions.question: The pH of the solution is 2 units above a side chain's pKa. What is mostly true of that group?
questions.explanation: From Henderson–Hasselbalch, 2 units above pKa gives [A⁻]/[HA] = 100, so ~99% deprotonated.

questions.question: At pH 7.4, which side chain is closest to being half protonated?
questions.explanation: His pKa is ~6, close to physiological pH, so a real fraction of it is protonated. That's why His shows up in pH-sensitive salt bridges.

questions.question: A carboxylic acid group at a pH BELOW its pKa has what charge?
questions.explanation: Below its pKa the acid keeps its H⁺ (COOH), so it's neutral.

questions.question: An amine group at a pH ABOVE its pKa has what charge?
questions.explanation: Above its pKa the amine loses its extra H⁺ (NH₃⁺ → NH₂), so it's neutral.

questions.question: What does the flat plateau on an amino acid titration curve represent?
options: The isoelectric point of the amino acid
A region of rapid pH change
A buffer region around a pKa
The point where all groups are charged
questions.explanation: Near a pKa, added base mostly converts HA to A⁻, so pH barely changes. That's the buffering plateau.

questions.question: A buffer has equal concentrations of acetic acid and acetate (pKa 4.76). What is the pH?
questions.explanation: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.76.

questions.question: Which are polar, uncharged amino acids? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Ser, Thr, Gln, Asn (plus Cys) are polar uncharged. Val is nonpolar; Asp is negatively charged.

questions.question: Which amino acid's side chain can form a covalent cross-link with another of its kind?
questions.explanation: Two Cys SH groups can be oxidized into a disulfide bond, which locks structure in place.

lessons.title: Peptide bonds and reading a sequence
lessons.search: peptide bond formation N terminus C terminus reading peptide sequence

blocks.p: A peptide bond joins the **carboxylic acid** of one amino acid to the **amine** of the next and kicks out water. That's a **condensation** reaction. In water (about 55 M water!) that's not favored on its own, so you have to **activate the carboxylic acid** to give it a good leaving group.

list: In the body, the carboxyl is activated with AMP and then tRNA. The ribosome holds everything in place.
The **growing chain carries the activated carboxyl**; the **new amino acid brings the amine**. So chains grow N → C.
In the lab you also need **protecting groups** so only the right ends react.

steps: Find the end with the free amine (NH₃⁺). That's the **N-terminus**, the start.
Find the end with the free carboxylate (COO⁻). That's the **C-terminus**.
Walk N → C, naming each side chain you pass.
Write it N → C in one-letter code.

blocks.key: Sequences are always written **N-terminus to C-terminus**, left to right. LAYGS and SGYAL are different peptides.

blocks.p: The peptide bond itself is **rigid and planar**. The chain can only twist at the α-carbons (the pivot points), which is why R groups control which folds are possible.

lessons.title: Finding the pI of a peptide, step by step
lessons.search: isoelectric point of a peptide calculation

blocks.p: pI = the pH where the peptide's **net charge is zero**. Dr. Tracy's method is a virtual titration. It always works.

steps: List the ionizable groups: the **N-terminus**, the **C-terminus**, and any ionizable **side chains** (D, E, H, C, Y, K, R). Ignore groups tied up in peptide bonds.
Put their pKa values in order, lowest to highest.
Start at very low pH where everything is protonated. Count the charge: each amine = +1, each acid = 0.
Step past each pKa one at a time. Passing an acid's pKa subtracts 1. Passing an amine's pKa also subtracts 1 (it goes +1 → 0).
Find the two pKa values on either side of the **net 0** region. **pI = their average.**

blocks.p: pKa: C-term 2.0, Asp 3.9, N-term 9.0, Lys 10.5.

example.q: Ala-Glu-Lys-Gly. pKa: N-term 9.0, C-term 2.0, Glu 4.1, Lys 10.5. pI?
K-R-G (Lys-Arg-Gly). pKa: C-term 2.0, N-term 9.0, Lys 10.5, Arg 12.5. pI?
example.a: Low pH: N-term +1, Lys +1, Arg +1 = +3. Past 2.0: +2. Past 9.0: +1. Past 10.5: 0. Past 12.5: −1. Zero is between 10.5 and 12.5, so pI = **11.5**. Lots of bases = high pI.

blocks.tip: Quick check: extra acidic side chains (D, E) pull the pI low. Extra basic ones (K, R) push it high. Your answer should make sense with that.

videos.title: Peptide isoelectric point with pI shortcut
Determining the isoelectric point of a polypeptide

questions.question: Peptide bond formation in water is unfavorable on its own. What strategy promotes it?
options: Activate the carboxylic acid with a leaving group
Protonate the amine so it becomes a better nucleophile
Remove a hydride from the α-carbon next to the carbonyl
Add extra water to push the equilibrium toward product
questions.explanation: It's a condensation making water, and water is ~55 M. Activating the carboxyl (AMP, then tRNA in cells) gives a good leaving group.

questions.question: During ribosomal synthesis, which piece carries the activated carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: The growing chain holds the activated carboxyl; the new amino acid supplies the amine, so the chain grows N → C.

questions.question: In which direction are peptide sequences written?
questions.explanation: Always N → C. Reversing the letters gives a different peptide.

questions.question: Why is the peptide bond itself rigid?
options: It is planar, with partial double-bond character
It is an ionic bond between the charged chain ends
It forms a disulfide bridge with its nearest neighbor
It is locked in place by H-bonds to nearby water
questions.explanation: The amide bond is planar and doesn't rotate freely. The chain twists at the α-carbons instead.

questions.question: A peptide is Asp-Ala-Lys. pKa values: C-term 2.0, Asp 3.9, N-term 9.0, Lys 10.5. What is its pI?
questions.explanation: Net charge goes +2, +1, 0, −1, −2 across the pKa's. Zero sits between 3.9 and 9.0: (3.9 + 9.0)/2 = 6.45.

questions.question: A peptide is Ala-Glu-Lys-Gly. pKa: N-term 9.0, C-term 2.0, Glu 4.1, Lys 10.5. What is its pI?
questions.explanation: Charges: +2, +1, 0, −1, −2. Zero between Glu (4.1) and N-term (9.0): pI = 6.55.

questions.question: A peptide is Lys-Arg-Gly. pKa: C-term 2.0, N-term 9.0, Lys 10.5, Arg 12.5. What is its pI?
questions.explanation: Low pH charge is +3. It drops to +2, +1, then 0 after 10.5. Zero between 10.5 and 12.5, so pI = 11.5.

questions.question: A peptide has three Glu residues and no basic side chains. Its pI will most likely be:
questions.explanation: Extra acidic side chains add negative charge, so you have to go to low pH to neutralize them. Low pI.

questions.question: At a pH above its pI, a peptide's net charge is:
questions.explanation: Above the pI more groups have lost H⁺, so the net charge is negative. Below the pI it's positive.

questions.question: When calculating a peptide's pI, which groups do you include?
options: Every amine and carboxyl in the chain, including those in peptide bonds
Only the ionizable side chains, ignoring both of the terminal groups
The free N-terminus, the free C-terminus, and ionizable side chains
Only the N-terminus and C-terminus, since side chains cancel out
questions.explanation: Groups in peptide bonds aren't ionizable. You count the two free termini plus any ionizable side chains.

questions.question: Which peptide is SGYAL written in three-letter code?
questions.explanation: S = Ser, G = Gly, Y = Tyr, A = Ala, L = Leu, written N → C.

questions.question: Which is Glu-Ile-Asn-Leu-Gly in one-letter code?
questions.explanation: Glu = E, Ile = I, Asn = N, Leu = L, Gly = G.

questions.question: You're given a drawn peptide structure. How do you find the first residue of the sequence?
options: Find the end with the free carboxylate group
Find the end with the free amine group
Find the residue with the largest side chain
Find the residue closest to any disulfide
questions.explanation: The free NH₃⁺ end is the N-terminus, which is where the sequence starts.

questions.question: What is the net charge of Asp-Ala-Lys at pH 7 (C-term 2.0, Asp 3.9, N-term 9.0, Lys 10.5)?
questions.explanation: At pH 7: C-term −1, Asp −1, N-term +1, Lys +1. Total is 0, which fits since its pI (6.45) is close to 7.

lessons.title: Picking a separation and how to get your protein off
lessons.search: protein purification chromatography ion exchange size exclusion affinity hydrophobic

blocks.p: Every separation uses one physical property: **size, charge (or pI), hydrophobicity, density, or binding (affinity)**. Match the property that makes your protein different from the junk, then know how to **elute** it (wash it off the column).

head: Method
Separates by
What sticks / moves
How you elute
rows: Raise salt, or raise pH so the protein loses + charge
Raise salt, or lower pH so the protein loses − charge
Small proteins wander into bead pores; **big ones come out first**
Just keep running buffer, nothing binds
Resin has an antibody or ligand for your protein
Add free ligand/competitor, or change pH or salt
Greasy C18 chains hold nonpolar proteins
Increase organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile). Often **kills activity** because organic solvent unfolds proteins
SDS unfolds and coats with − charge; **small runs farther**
Protein moves in a pH gradient until it hits its pI and stops

blocks.key: Charge trick: at a pH **below** its pI a protein is **positive** (use cation exchange). **Above** its pI it's **negative** (use anion exchange).

example.q: Your protein has pI 9. Contaminants have pI around 5. You run a column at pH 7. Which column, and how do you elute?
example.a: At pH 7 your protein is below its pI, so it's **positive**. Contaminants are above theirs, so they're negative and flow through. Use **cation exchange** (negative resin), then elute with a **salt gradient** (or raise the pH).

blocks.tip: SDS-PAGE caveat from class: distance traveled isn't perfectly linear with MW, so estimates are approximate.

blocks.p: General purification plan from class: (1) break cells open while protecting the protein, (2) use a physical/chemical difference to separate, (3) track where your protein went (A280 absorbance, specific activity, or antibody recognition), (4) repeat 2 and 3.

videos.title: Protein Purification: affinity, ion exchange, hydrophobic interaction, size exclusion

lessons.title: Specific activity and designing an activity assay
lessons.search: specific activity enzyme purification table explained

blocks.p: **Specific activity = activity ÷ total protein** (units per mg). It tells you how much of the protein in your tube is actually your working enzyme.
You lost some total activity (12 → 9), but you threw out a lot of junk protein, so specific activity went **up**. That means purity went up.

blocks.key: Purification working = specific activity rising. But purity can go up while specific activity **drops** if the step destroys folding or strips a cofactor (hydrophobic columns with organic solvent do this).

blocks.p: If they give you a protein's job, you design a way to watch that job happen:

steps: Pick something you can measure: **substrate disappearing or product appearing**. Best if one of them absorbs light or fluoresces (a **spectroscopic assay**, using A = εbc).
Mix a known amount of protein with substrate at a fixed pH and temperature.
Measure the signal **over time** and take the early, straight-line rate.
Run **controls**: no enzyme, and heat-killed enzyme, so you know the change is really from your protein.
Divide the rate (units) by mg protein for specific activity.

example.q: An enzyme converts a colorless substrate into a yellow product that absorbs at 405 nm. How would you measure its activity?
example.a: Mix enzyme with substrate, then track **absorbance at 405 nm over time**. The early slope is the rate of product formation. Include a no-enzyme control. Divide by mg of protein to get specific activity.

questions.question: A protein is positively charged at pH 7. Which column will bind it?
options: Anion exchange, with a positive resin
Cation exchange, with a negative resin
Size exclusion, with a porous resin
Reversed phase, with a C18 resin
questions.explanation: Positive proteins stick to a negative resin, which is cation exchange (it exchanges cations).

questions.question: A protein with a net negative charge at pH 7 would bind to:
questions.explanation: Anion exchange resins are positive and bind negative proteins.

questions.question: A protein bound to a cation exchange column can be eluted by:
options: Lowering the pH of the buffer
Adding more of the same protein
questions.explanation: Salt cations compete for the negative resin and knock the protein off. (Raising pH also works by removing the protein's + charge.)

questions.question: In size exclusion chromatography, which proteins come off the column first?
questions.explanation: Large proteins can't enter the bead pores, so they take the short path and elute first.

questions.question: Why does hydrophobic (reversed phase) chromatography often destroy specific activity?
options: Organic solvent in the mobile phase unfolds it
The C18 resin cleaves peptide bonds in the protein
The salt gradient strips away every bound cofactor
The column sorts proteins by charge instead of polarity
questions.explanation: Eluting needs organic solvent, which disrupts the hydration cage and unfolds proteins. Lose the fold, lose the activity.

questions.question: What does SDS do in SDS-PAGE?
options: Folds proteins back into their native, active shape
Unfolds proteins and coats them in negative charge
Binds only positively charged proteins and holds them
Separates proteins by their isoelectric point in a gel
questions.explanation: SDS denatures and gives a uniform negative charge per length, so proteins separate by size alone.

questions.question: Which technique separates proteins based on their isoelectric point?
questions.explanation: In IEF each protein migrates through a pH gradient until it reaches its pI, where net charge is 0, and stops.

questions.question: Ultracentrifugation separates proteins and complexes by:
questions.explanation: Samples settle to the layer matching their density.

questions.question: Your target has pI 9.5; most contaminants have pI near 5. You run at pH 7. What's the best first step?
options: Cation exchange, then elute with a salt gradient
Anion exchange, then elute with a salt gradient
Reversed phase, then elute with acetonitrile
Size exclusion, since charge will not matter
questions.explanation: At pH 7 the target is below its pI (positive) and contaminants are above theirs (negative). Cation exchange grabs just the target.

questions.question: A His-tagged protein is bound to a nickel affinity column. How is it most directly eluted?
options: Add a competitor that binds the resin
Add SDS to coat it with negative charge
Spin the column in an ultracentrifuge
Lower the salt to strengthen binding
questions.explanation: Affinity columns release the protein when you add something that competes for the binding site (imidazole for His tags) or change pH.

questions.question: Before a column: 1 mg protein, 12 units of activity. After: 0.5 mg, 9 units. What is the new specific activity?
questions.explanation: Specific activity = 9 units ÷ 0.5 mg = 18 units/mg. It went up, so purity improved.

questions.question: Can a purification step raise purity but lower specific activity?
options: No, purity and specific activity always rise together
Yes, if the step destroys folding or removes a cofactor
No, specific activity only depends on protein mass
Yes, but only if the protein is measured by SDS-PAGE
questions.explanation: Specific activity only counts working enzyme. If the step unfolds it or strips a cofactor, purity can rise while activity falls.

questions.question: You're designing an assay for an enzyme that makes a colored product. Which belong in a good design? (Select all that apply)
options: Use the final reading after a day
Normalize the rate to mg of protein
questions.explanation: Watch the product form over time, use the early rate, control for non-enzyme changes, hold conditions steady, and divide by mg for specific activity.

questions.question: Which properties can be used to purify a protein from a crude extract? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: All of them. That's why knowing a protein's physical properties matters. (This one is a slide question.)

questions.question: Which step comes FIRST in a general purification scheme?
options: Run an SDS-PAGE gel to find the target protein
Release the protein from cells while protecting it
Measure the specific activity of every fraction
Elute the target protein with organic solvent
questions.explanation: First liberate it from the cell or tissue without wrecking it, then separate, then track it, then repeat.

lessons.title: MS1 vs MS2, and b and y ions
lessons.search: tandem mass spectrometry b ions y ions peptide sequencing

list: **MS1**: measures the mass-to-charge (m/z) of the **whole, intact peptides** in the sample. It's the list of what's there.
**MS2** (tandem MS): one ion from MS1 is picked, **broken apart**, and the **fragments** are measured. Fragments tell you the sequence.

blocks.p: The peptide usually breaks at a peptide bond, giving two pieces:

list: **b ions** keep the charge on the **N-terminal** piece. b1 = first residue, b2 = first two, and so on.
**y ions** keep the charge on the **C-terminal** piece. y1 = last residue, y2 = last two, and so on.

blocks.key: The mass **difference between neighboring ions** (b3 − b2, or y4 − y3) equals the mass of one residue. Read the ladder and you read the sequence.

blocks.p: A few residue masses (you'd be given a table): Gly 57, Ala 71, **Ser 87**, Pro 97, Val 99, Thr 101, **Leu/Ile 113**, **Gln/Lys 128**, Glu 129, Phe 147, **Tyr 163**, Trp 186.

blocks.tip: Leu and Ile weigh the same (113), and Gln and Lys are nearly the same (128). You need context, like the known protein sequence, to tell them apart. Dr. Tracy's slide example used exactly this.

blocks.p: A modification like phosphorylation adds mass (+80). Every fragment that **contains** the modified residue gets heavier. Every fragment that doesn't, stays the same. So find where the shift starts.

example.q: Peptide G-A-L-S-K. After treatment, b1–b3 are unchanged, but b4 and up are +80. Which residue is modified? What would y1 and y2 do?
example.a: The shift starts at b4, and residue 4 is **Ser**. y1 (just K) doesn't contain Ser, so it's unchanged. y2 (S-K) contains it, so y2 is +80.

example.q: Peptide A-Y-G-T-R. y1, y2, y3 are unchanged, but y4 is +80. Which residue?
example.a: y4 = Y-G-T-R, y3 = G-T-R. The only new residue in y4 is **Tyr** (position 2).

videos.title: Mass spectrometry for proteomics, part 2
De novo peptide sequencing from mass spectrometry data

blocks.p: Edman degradation is the **chemical** way to sequence, one residue at a time from the **N-terminus**.

steps: **PITC** (phenyl isothiocyanate) reacts with the free N-terminal amine.
Mild acid cleaves off just that first residue as a labeled derivative.
Identify it by chromatography.
The rest of the peptide now has a new N-terminus. Repeat.

head: Edman
Mass spec
rows: Lots of single backbone breaks at once

blocks.p: Why was insulin so hard for Sanger? It has **disulfide bonds**, which react with the sequencing chemistry, and two chains. You have to break the disulfides first (a **reduction** reaction).

blocks.key: Edman = N-terminal, stepwise, PITC, needs pure protein. Mass spec = fast, handles mixtures, reads b/y ladders.

videos.title: Protein Sequencing: Edman Degradation
Amino Acid Sequencing and Edman Degradation

questions.question: What does MS1 measure in a peptide mass spec experiment?
options: The masses of intact peptide ions in the sample
The masses of fragments from one chosen peptide
The charge of each amino acid side chain
The order of residues by chemical labeling
questions.explanation: MS1 surveys the intact peptides. MS2 fragments a chosen one.

questions.question: In MS2, what happens to the ion chosen from MS1?
options: It is broken into fragments that are measured
It is labeled with PITC and then cleaved off
It is separated by its isoelectric point first
It is denatured with SDS and run on a gel
questions.explanation: The chosen precursor is fragmented, and the b and y fragments reveal its sequence.

questions.question: Which statement about b ions is true?
options: They keep the charge on the C-terminal piece
They are used to find the end of the peptide
They keep the charge on the N-terminal piece
They are not useful for sequencing
questions.explanation: b ions are N-terminal fragments; y ions are C-terminal fragments.

questions.question: Two neighboring b ions differ by 87 mass units. Which residue was added? (Gly 57, Ser 87, Pro 97, Thr 101)
questions.explanation: The gap between neighboring ions equals one residue's mass. 87 = Ser.

questions.question: Neighboring y ions differ by 163. Which residue is it? (Phe 147, Tyr 163, Trp 186, His 137)
Peptide G-A-L-S-K. After a kinase treatment, b1–b3 are unchanged but b4 and larger b ions are +80. Which residue is phosphorylated?
questions.explanation: The shift first appears in b4, so residue 4 carries the +80. That's Ser.

questions.question: Same peptide, G-A-L-S-K, phosphorylated on Ser. Which y ion is the smallest one that shows the +80 shift?
questions.explanation: y1 is just K. y2 is S-K, the first y ion that contains the Ser, so it's the first to shift.

questions.question: Peptide A-Y-G-T-R. y1, y2, and y3 are unchanged, but y4 is +80. Which residue is modified?
questions.explanation: y4 (YGTR) adds Tyr to y3 (GTR). Only Tyr is new, so Tyr carries the modification.

questions.question: Why can't a basic MS2 ladder tell leucine from isoleucine?
questions.explanation: Leu and Ile are isomers (both 113). You need extra context, like the known protein sequence.

questions.question: Edman degradation removes and identifies residues from which end?
options: The C-terminus, one at a time
The N-terminus, one at a time
Both ends at once, in pairs
questions.explanation: PITC labels the free N-terminal amine; that residue is cleaved off and identified, then repeat.

questions.question: What reagent labels the N-terminal amino acid in Edman degradation?
questions.explanation: Phenyl isothiocyanate (PITC).

questions.question: Why was Edman sequencing so difficult for insulin?
options: Disulfides react with the sequencing agents
It has too many reactive N-terminal groups
It has too many reactive C-terminal groups
It is too hydrophobic to dissolve in buffer
questions.explanation: That's the slide answer: disulfides interfere. They must be broken (reduced) first.

questions.question: For which method is protein purity most critical?
questions.explanation: Chemical sequencing needs one pure peptide or the signals mix. Mass spec can sort a mixture in MS1.

questions.question: Which are ways to determine a protein's primary sequence? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Edman and MS both read sequence by breaking amide bonds. Size exclusion and IEF only separate.

lessons.title: α-helix: the i → i+3/i+4 rule
lessons.search: alpha helix structure hydrogen bonding i i+4 side chain interactions

blocks.p: In an α-helix the backbone coils up and **backbone C=O and N-H groups H-bond** along the helix. Side chains stick **out**.

list: About **3.6 residues per turn**, mostly **right-handed** (because of L amino acids).
Residues **3 to 4 apart (i and i+3/i+4)** end up on the **same face** of the helix, right next to each other.

blocks.key: To predict helix stability, look at pairs 3–4 residues apart. **Opposite charges** (like E at i, K at i+4) or **two hydrophobics** = stabilizing. **Same charges** = repulsion, destabilizing.

list: **Proline**: its side chain is locked into a ring with its own backbone N, so it has **no N-H to H-bond** and it forces a kink.
**Glycine**: way too flexible. Pinning it in a helix costs a lot of entropy, so it prefers loops and turns.
A long run of the **same charge** (like EEEE or KKKK) repels itself.

example.q: Why is G-P-D-W-S-P-Y-G-A unlikely to form an α-helix?
example.a: It's loaded with **Pro** (breaks H-bonding, kinks the chain) and **Gly** (too flexible). Those are classic helix breakers.

example.q: Which helix is more stable: one with Glu at position 3 and Lys at position 7, or Glu at 3 and Glu at 7?
example.a: Glu 3 / Lys 7. They're 4 apart, same face, and opposite charges form a salt bridge. Glu/Glu would repel.

videos.title: Protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary

lessons.title: β-strands: every other residue
lessons.search: beta sheet structure alternating side chains parallel antiparallel

blocks.p: β-strands are stretched-out chains that line up side by side into a **β-sheet**. The H-bonds are between the **backbones of neighboring strands**.

list: Side chains **alternate up, down, up, down**. So **every other residue** (i, i+2) lands on the same face.
Sheets can be **parallel** or **antiparallel**. **β-turns** (often with Gly and Pro) hairpin one strand back into the next, which is how antiparallel sheets get made.
Classic pattern: alternating hydrophobic/polar, so one face is greasy (buried) and the other faces water.

blocks.key: For sheet stability, look at residues **2 apart**. Opposite charges or matched hydrophobics at i and i+2 = stabilizing. Same charges at i and i+2 = repulsion.

example.q: Slide quiz: which favors a β-sheet, Leu-Arg-Gly-Lys or Leu-Arg-Gly-Glu?
example.a: **Leu-Arg-Gly-Glu**. Arg and Glu are 2 apart (same face) with opposite charges, so they make an ionic bond. Arg and Lys would repel.

example.q: Why might D-V-E-H-D-K-E-W-D-V struggle to form a stable β-sheet?
example.a: It's packed with charged residues, many of the same sign on the same face (D, E, D, E, D), so there's a lot of charge repulsion and little hydrophobic face to bury.

blocks.p: Two Cys can link covalently (an oxidation). That locks structure and **reduces motion**. Breaking one open is a **reduction**.

questions.question: What H-bonds stabilize an α-helix?
options: Side chain to side chain bonds
questions.explanation: The helix is held by backbone amide H-bonds along the coil. R groups point outward.

questions.question: In an α-helix, which residue positions sit next to each other on the same face?
questions.explanation: With ~3.6 residues per turn, residues 3–4 apart line up on the same side.

questions.question: In a β-strand, which residues point to the same side of the sheet?
questions.explanation: Side chains alternate up and down, so i and i+2 share a face.

questions.question: Which pair would most stabilize an α-helix?
options: Glu at position 5, Lys at position 9
Glu at position 5, Glu at position 9
Lys at position 5, Lys at position 9
Glu at position 5, Lys at position 6
questions.explanation: 5 and 9 are 4 apart, on the same face, and opposite charges form a salt bridge.

questions.question: Why does proline disrupt α-helices?
options: Its ring locks the backbone and removes the amide N-H
It carries a negative charge that repels its neighbors
It is so flexible that holding it in place costs entropy
It forms disulfide bonds with nearby cysteine residues
questions.explanation: Pro's side chain loops back onto its own N, removing the H-bond donor and forcing a kink.

questions.question: Why does glycine tend to destabilize α-helices?
options: Its bulky side chain clashes with the backbone
It is so flexible that fixing it costs entropy
It carries a positive charge at physiological pH
It cannot form peptide bonds with its neighbors
questions.explanation: Gly has no side chain, so it can adopt many angles. Freezing it into a helix costs a lot of entropy.

questions.question: A 10-residue peptide is G-P-D-W-S-P-Y-G-A. Why is it unlikely to form an α-helix?
options: It has several Pro and Gly residues
It is too hydrophobic to stay in water
It has too many opposite charges
It contains no amino acids with rings
questions.explanation: Pro and Gly are the classic helix breakers.

questions.question: Which primary structure would favor a β-sheet?
questions.explanation: Arg and Glu are 2 apart (same face) and oppositely charged: an ionic bond. Arg/Lys would repel.

questions.question: A peptide D-V-E-H-D-K-E-W-D-V is unlikely to form a stable β-sheet mainly because:
options: Many same-charged residues repel on the same face
It is too short for any backbone H-bonds
It has too many Pro residues breaking strands
Its hydrophobic residues all line up perfectly
questions.explanation: Lots of D and E on alternating positions means charge repulsion and not much hydrophobic face to bury.

questions.question: Most α-helices in proteins are right-handed because:
options: Proteins are built from L amino acids
Disulfide bonds twist to the right
questions.explanation: The L configuration of the α-carbons makes the right-handed helix the favorable one.

questions.question: β-turns are most associated with which type of β-sheet?
questions.explanation: A tight β-turn hairpins a strand back on itself, lining up antiparallel strands.

questions.question: What type of reaction opens a disulfide bond?
questions.explanation: Disulfides form by oxidation and are broken by reduction.

questions.question: Which would DESTABILIZE an α-helix? (Select all that apply)
options: Lys at i, i+4, and i+8
A Pro in the middle of the helix
Glu at i and Lys at i+4
Several Gly residues in a row
Leu at i and Ile at i+4
questions.explanation: Same-charge repulsion, Pro, and Gly all hurt helices. E/K at i and i+4 or two hydrophobics at i and i+4 help.

questions.question: What does a disulfide bond do to a protein's structure?
options: Reduces motion and locks the fold
questions.explanation: The covalent cross-link restrains how the chain can move, stabilizing tertiary or quaternary structure.

lessons.title: Four levels of structure and what holds them together
lessons.search: protein structure primary secondary tertiary quaternary folding hydrophobic

head: Level
What it is
Held by
rows: Local backbone patterns: α-helix, β-sheet, turns
The full 3D fold of **one** polypeptide chain
Hydrophobic effect, H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulfides

blocks.p: Hemoglobin (α₂β₂, four chains) has quaternary structure. Myoglobin (one chain) doesn't.

list: **Hydrophobic effect**: the main driving force. Greasy residues get buried inside, polar ones face water. Entropy of water again.

**Ionic bonds (salt bridges)** and **H-bonds**: they mostly set the **correct orientation** and specificity. The slide line: "Ionic or H-bonds frequently participate in correct orientation, but the driving force is primarily entropy."
**Disulfides**: covalent locks that cut down motion.

blocks.key: Mutation logic: swapping a buried hydrophobic for a charged residue, or breaking a salt bridge, lowers stability. Adding a matched salt bridge or better-packed hydrophobic core raises it.

list: Folding starts **while the chain is still coming off the ribosome**.
It can't try every shape (that's **Levinthal's paradox**). Instead **hydrophobic collapse** happens fast, then 2° structure forms, then motifs, then the final fold at the **lowest ΔG**.
About 25–30% of proteins need **chaperones**, which protect hydrophobic surfaces and guide folding.
Misfolding: **amyloid** (Alzheimer's) is stacked **β-sheets** driven by hydrophobic interactions. **Prions** are misfolded proteins that convert normal copies into the misfolded form.

example.q: A mutation swaps a Leu buried in the core for an Asp. Predict the effect and explain.
example.a: Less stable. Asp is charged and wants water. Burying it costs a lot, and you lose the water-entropy gain the Leu provided. The protein may partly unfold.

videos.title: Protein Folding & Quaternary Structure
Protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary

lessons.title: Brownian motion, the ratchet, and evolution

blocks.p: Everything in a protein is constantly jiggling from heat. That random vibration is **Brownian motion**. The **bonds in the protein** (backbone, salt bridges, disulfides, bound ligands) decide **which** jiggles are allowed.

Random shaking goes nowhere on its own. But if you **block motion in the other directions** and couple it to something that's out of equilibrium (like a concentration difference), random motion turns into **directed work**. That's a **Brownian ratchet**.
Dr. Tracy's sand analogy: shake a box of sand and a light ball rises to the top, a heavy ball sinks. The shaking is random; the direction comes from the constraint.

blocks.key: Change the bonding → change the allowed motion → change the function. Example: salt bridges in hemoglobin restrict motion and hold the T state. Break them and the protein can move into the R state.

blocks.p: When a ligand binds, both the protein and the ligand shift shape a bit to fit better. That small change can **spread across the whole protein** (hemoglobin, and the antibody-angiogenin homework example).

head: Divergent
Convergent
rows: Similar 3D structure/fold even though sequence drifted apart
Different overall folds that arrive at a similar function or active site
Myoglobin and hemoglobin: only ~18% sequence identity but nearly the same fold
Unrelated enzymes that independently evolved similar catalytic sites

blocks.tip: Structure is conserved much better than sequence. Low sequence identity with a matching fold still points to **divergent** evolution.

questions.question: What is tertiary structure?
options: The amino acid sequence of the chain
Local helices and sheets along the backbone
The full 3D fold of a single polypeptide
The arrangement of several separate chains
questions.explanation: Tertiary = the complete fold of one chain. Quaternary = how multiple chains fit together.

questions.question: Which protein has quaternary structure?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin has four subunits (α₂β₂). Myoglobin is one chain.

questions.question: What is the main driving force of protein folding in water?
options: The hydrophobic effect, from water entropy
Ionic attraction between all charged groups
questions.explanation: Burying nonpolar residues frees water. Ionic and H-bonds mainly set orientation.

questions.question: According to the course, what role do ionic and H-bonds usually play in protein-protein interactions?
options: They are the primary driving force of binding
They set correct orientation and specificity
They stop mattering once folding has started
They only matter in fully denatured proteins
questions.explanation: Slide wording: they frequently participate in correct orientation, but the driving force is primarily entropy.

questions.question: A buried Leu in the core is mutated to Asp. What is the most likely result?
options: The quaternary structure is unaffected by design
The protein gains a new disulfide bond
questions.explanation: A charged residue buried away from water is costly and removes a hydrophobic contribution.

questions.question: Levinthal's paradox points out that:
options: Proteins can't fold by testing every shape at random
Proteins only fold after they have left the cell
Folding always needs a chaperone to finish correctly
Unfolded chains have lower entropy than folded ones
questions.explanation: There are far too many conformations to test. Folding follows a guided path: hydrophobic collapse, 2° structure, then the fold.

questions.question: What is a key role of chaperone proteins?
options: Protect hydrophobic surfaces and guide folding
Covalently bond to the protein's active site
Break peptide bonds in misfolded proteins
Add phosphate groups to finished proteins
questions.explanation: Chaperones shield exposed hydrophobic patches and steer proteins toward the native state.

questions.question: Amyloid fibrils are primarily composed of:
questions.explanation: Amyloid is stacked β-sheet structure, driven largely by hydrophobic interactions.

questions.question: What makes prions unusual?
options: A misfolded copy converts normal ones into misfolded ones
They can only fold while they are bound to a chaperone
They are proteins built entirely out of D amino acids
They lack both tertiary and quaternary structure entirely
questions.explanation: The misfolded prion acts as a template, spreading misfolding.

questions.question: What does Brownian motion mean in the context of protein function?
options: Random thermal jiggling, limited by the protein's bonds
Directed motion that is powered only by ATP hydrolysis
The slow drift of proteins toward the nucleus over time
Motion caused by gravity pulling on very large proteins
questions.explanation: Heat makes everything vibrate; the bonds in the protein decide which motions are allowed.

questions.question: What turns random Brownian motion into a directional 'ratchet' that does work?
options: Blocking motion in other directions and coupling it to a non-equilibrium process
Raising the temperature until the vibrations turn directional entirely on their own
Removing all of the bonds so the protein is free to move in every possible direction
Adding more water so that collisions happen more often from every direction at once
questions.explanation: Constrain the allowed motions and couple to something out of equilibrium, and random motion becomes directed.

questions.question: Adding a disulfide bond to a flexible loop would most likely:
options: Restrict the loop's motion and possibly change function
Increase the loop's motion and overall flexibility
Have no effect, since disulfide bonds are very weak
Turn the flexible loop into a β-sheet right away
questions.explanation: New covalent bonds cut down allowed motion. Change the allowed motion, change the function.

questions.question: Myoglobin and hemoglobin share ~18% sequence identity but nearly identical folds. This is evidence of:
questions.explanation: Same fold from a common ancestor while the sequence drifted: divergent.

questions.question: Two unrelated proteins with totally different folds both evolved a similar catalytic site. This is:
questions.explanation: Different starting points arriving at the same solution is convergent evolution.

questions.question: The induced fit model says:
options: The protein is rigid and never changes its shape
Only the ligand changes shape to fit the protein
Both protein and ligand shift to optimize binding
Binding happens only through new covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Both partners adjust. And the change can spread across the protein.

lessons.title: Kd, θ, and reading a binding curve
lessons.search: dissociation constant Kd fractional saturation binding curve

blocks.p: Binding is an equilibrium: **P + L ⇌ PL**.

list: **Kd = [P][L] / [PL] = 1/Ka**. It's the **dissociation** constant.
**θ** (theta) = fraction of binding sites filled. **θ = [L] / ([L] + Kd)**.
Plug in [L] = Kd and you get θ = 0.5. So **Kd is the ligand concentration where half the sites are full**.

blocks.key: **Low Kd = high affinity** (it only takes a little ligand to fill half the sites). **High Kd = low affinity.** They're inversely related.

steps: Find θ = 0.5 on the y-axis (the halfway line).
Go across to the curve, then straight down to the x-axis.
That x-value is the Kd. The curve that hits halfway **farther left** has the **lower Kd and higher affinity**.

blocks.p: For gases like O₂, the x-axis is partial pressure (pO₂) instead of concentration, and the halfway point is often called P50. Same idea.

example.q: Protein X reaches θ = 0.5 at 2 µM ligand. Protein Y reaches it at 20 µM. Which binds tighter?
example.a: **Protein X**. Its Kd (2 µM) is lower, so it has higher affinity.

list: **Enzymes** use induced fit to favor the **transition state** and promote chemistry.
**Antibodies** use induced fit to hold the **bound structure** tightly and specifically.

videos.title: Kd (dissociation constant) and binding affinity: what, why, and how to interpret

questions.question: What does a low Kd indicate?
questions.explanation: Low Kd means little ligand is needed to fill half the sites: tight binding.

questions.question: At what ligand concentration is θ = 0.5?
questions.explanation: θ = [L]/([L] + Kd). When [L] = Kd, θ = Kd/2Kd = 0.5.

questions.question: Which is the correct expression for Kd of P + L ⇌ PL?
questions.explanation: Kd = [P][L]/[PL], the inverse of Ka.

questions.question: How are Kd and Ka related?
questions.explanation: Kd is the dissociation constant; Ka is association. They are reciprocals.

questions.question: Protein X reaches half saturation at 2 µM ligand; Protein Y at 20 µM. Which statement is true?
options: X has the higher Kd and higher affinity
X has the lower Kd and higher affinity
Y has the lower Kd and higher affinity
X and Y have equal affinity
questions.explanation: Half saturation happens at [L] = Kd. X's Kd is lower, so X binds tighter.

questions.question: On a θ vs [L] plot, how do you read the Kd?
options: Find where the curve starts rising from zero
Find the maximum θ the curve reaches
Find the slope at the very first point
questions.explanation: Kd is the ligand concentration at half saturation.

questions.question: If Kd = 10 µM and [L] = 10 µM, what fraction of sites are occupied?
questions.explanation: [L] = Kd gives θ = 0.5.

questions.question: If Kd = 10 µM and [L] = 90 µM, what is θ?
For a gas like O₂, what is usually on the x-axis of a binding curve?
questions.explanation: Gases are measured as partial pressure, so Kd is read in pressure units.

questions.question: How does an enzyme use induced fit differently from an antibody?
options: An enzyme stabilizes the transition state; an antibody holds the bound form
An enzyme stays rigid; an antibody changes shape to fit its target
An enzyme binds covalently; an antibody binds only through water entropy
An enzyme lowers Kd to zero; an antibody always raises its Kd
questions.explanation: Enzymes use induced fit to promote chemistry via the transition state. Antibodies use it for tight, specific binding.

questions.question: Which statements about Kd are true? (Select all that apply)
options: It is intrinsic to that protein-ligand pair
It is inversely related to binding affinity
questions.explanation: Kd is intrinsic to the pair, inversely related to affinity, and read at θ = 0.5. Higher affinity means LOWER Kd.

questions.question: A change to a protein makes it need MORE ligand to reach half saturation. What happened?
questions.explanation: Needing more ligand for θ = 0.5 means a higher Kd, which means lower affinity.

lessons.title: Myoglobin vs hemoglobin, and the heme
lessons.search: myoglobin vs hemoglobin structure cooperativity heme proximal distal histidine

head: Myoglobin
Hemoglobin
rows: Carry O₂ from lungs to tissues

blocks.p: Both have nearly the same helical fold holding a **heme** (a porphyrin ring with an **Fe²⁺** in the middle). That's the divergent evolution example.

list: **Proximal His**: bonded directly to the iron, underneath the heme.

**Distal His**: on the O₂ side. It **H-bonds to bound O₂** (boosts O₂ affinity) and forces ligands to bind at an angle, which **cuts down CO binding**. CO still binds much tighter than O₂, which is why it's toxic.

blocks.p: When one subunit binds O₂, the others get **higher** affinity. That's what makes the curve S-shaped. It lets hemoglobin load up fully in the lungs (high pO₂) and dump a big chunk of O₂ in tissues (low pO₂). Myoglobin's hyperbolic curve would just hang onto it.

blocks.key: Cooperative = binding at one site increases affinity at the others. Sigmoidal curve = big change in saturation over a small change in pO₂ = efficient delivery.

videos.title: Hemoglobin part 1: cooperative binding, allostery and 2,3-BPG

lessons.title: T state, R state, and what shifts them
lessons.search: hemoglobin T state R state Bohr effect BPG CO2 temperature

steps: O₂ binds and pulls the Fe **into the plane** of the heme (heme flattens).
The Fe drags the **proximal His** with it, which moves the whole **F helix** like a lever.
That shift travels to the **α₁β₂ / α₂β₁ interfaces**, which slide and rotate about 15°.
Salt bridges holding T break, the other subunits switch to R, and their affinity goes up. That's cooperativity.

blocks.h: Things that stabilize T (lower affinity, help release O₂)

head: Factor
How it works
rows: Protonates groups like His, strengthening the pH-sensitive salt bridges that hold T
Reacts with the N-termini to form **carbamates** (+ charge becomes −), making new salt bridges. CO₂ also makes H⁺ (carbonic acid → bicarbonate), which lowers pH
Fits in the central cavity between the β subunits (positive Lys/His pocket), only in T. More BPG = lower affinity. Levels shift over ~3 days (altitude)
O₂ binding is **exothermic**, so adding heat pushes the equilibrium toward release

blocks.key: Active tissue is warm, acidic, and full of CO₂. Every one of those stabilizes the T state, raises the Kd, and makes hemoglobin **drop O₂ exactly where it's needed**.

blocks.p: **Fetal hemoglobin** swaps β for γ subunits, which bind BPG poorly. So fetal Hb has **higher affinity** than mom's and can pull O₂ across the placenta.

example.q: If the Lys residues in the BPG pocket were mutated to neutral residues, what happens to O₂ affinity?
example.a: BPG (very negative) can't bind well, so T isn't stabilized as much. **Affinity goes up** (Kd goes down), and O₂ delivery to tissues gets worse.

videos.title: Biochemistry of Hemoglobin: Bohr effect, cooperativity, and 2,3-BPG

questions.question: What best describes cooperativity in hemoglobin?
options: O₂ binding decreases affinity at other sites
O₂ binding increases affinity at other sites
questions.explanation: Once one subunit binds O₂, the others shift toward R and bind more easily.

questions.question: Compared to myoglobin, hemoglobin's O₂ binding curve is:
questions.explanation: Hb is cooperative (S-shaped) and has a higher Kd than Mb.

questions.question: Which state of hemoglobin has LOW oxygen affinity?
questions.explanation: T (tense) = low affinity, favored in tissues. R (relaxed) = high affinity, favored in lungs.

questions.question: When O₂ binds heme, what happens to the iron?
options: It is pulled into the plane of the heme
It is pushed out of the plane of the heme
It changes from Fe²⁺ to Fe⁴⁺ permanently
It detaches from the proximal histidine
questions.explanation: The Fe moves into the plane, flattening the heme and dragging the proximal His and F helix.

questions.question: If the proximal His pulls the iron toward a puckered (non-planar) heme, how do affinity and Kd change?
questions.explanation: Puckered heme = T state stabilized = lower affinity = higher Kd. (Slide quiz.)

questions.question: Which histidine H-bonds to bound O₂ and reduces CO affinity by forcing angled binding?
questions.explanation: The distal His sits on the O₂ side of the heme.

questions.question: Where does most of the T → R rearrangement happen?
options: At the α₁β₂ and α₂β₁ interfaces
Between the two α subunits only
At the C-terminus of a single chain
questions.explanation: The subunit interfaces slide and rotate about 15° during the switch.

questions.question: How does BPG lower hemoglobin's O₂ affinity?
options: It binds the central cavity and stabilizes T
It binds heme iron in place of oxygen itself
It raises the pH inside the red blood cells
It forms carbamates on the chain N-termini
questions.explanation: BPG fits between the β subunits only in the T state, holding hemoglobin there.

questions.question: Why does heat decrease hemoglobin's O₂ affinity?
options: O₂ binding is exothermic, so heat favors release
Heat protonates the distal histidine side chain
Heat breaks the porphyrin ring into fragments
Heat converts all of the Fe²⁺ into Fe³⁺ at once
questions.explanation: Binding releases heat (−ΔH). Adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward unbinding.

questions.question: How does high CO₂ stabilize the T state?
options: It forms carbamates on N-termini, making salt bridges
It binds the heme iron and blocks the O₂ binding site
It fills the BPG pocket and pushes BPG out of the way
It raises the pH so every salt bridge is broken apart
questions.explanation: Carbamates turn + N-termini negative, making new salt bridges that favor T. CO₂ also lowers pH.

questions.question: Which conditions most strongly promote the T state in peripheral tissues?
options: High pH, low CO₂, low temperature
Low pH, high CO₂, high temperature
High pH, high CO₂, low BPG
Low pH, low CO₂, low temperature
questions.explanation: Active tissue is acidic, CO₂-rich, and warm. All stabilize T and promote O₂ release.

questions.question: What is the Bohr effect?
options: Lower pH decreases hemoglobin's O₂ affinity
Lower pH increases hemoglobin's O₂ affinity
questions.explanation: More H⁺ strengthens pH-sensitive salt bridges that hold T, so O₂ is released more easily.

questions.question: Why does fetal hemoglobin have higher O₂ affinity than adult hemoglobin?
options: Its γ subunits bind BPG poorly
It has no heme groups at all
questions.explanation: Fetal Hb uses γ instead of β. It binds BPG less, so it stays higher affinity and can take O₂ from the mother.

questions.question: The Lys residues in hemoglobin's BPG pocket are mutated to neutral residues. What happens?
options: BPG binds better and O₂ affinity drops
BPG binds worse and O₂ affinity rises
Nothing changes since BPG binds heme
questions.explanation: BPG is very negative and needs those + charges. Without them, T isn't stabilized as well, so affinity rises.

questions.question: Why does a sigmoidal binding curve help O₂ delivery?
options: Saturation changes a lot between lung and tissue pO₂
It keeps hemoglobin fully saturated inside tissues
It means hemoglobin never lets go of O₂ in the lungs
It makes hemoglobin's Kd the same as myoglobin's
questions.explanation: The steep middle of the S-curve sits in the tissue pO₂ range, so a lot of O₂ unloads there.

lessons.title: How westerns and ELISAs use antibodies

blocks.p: Antibodies bind one specific spot on a target (the **epitope**) with high affinity. Both assays use that to find and measure a protein.

steps: Run the sample on **SDS-PAGE** so proteins separate by size.
Transfer the proteins onto a membrane.
**Primary antibody** binds your target. That gives **selectivity**.
**Secondary antibody** (it recognizes the primary's constant region) carries a label or enzyme. That gives **sensitivity** (signal amplification).
You see a band: tells you the protein is **present** and its **size**.

blocks.p: Built for **lots of samples** on a plate. Two designs from class:

list: **Sandwich** (signal rises): capture antibody stuck to the plate → target binds → labeled detection antibody binds the target → wash → color. More target = more signal.
**Competitive** (signal falls): your target blocks a labeled molecule from binding. More target = **less** signal.

blocks.p: Targets can be proteins, lipids, or hormones (like testosterone in the saliva activity).

blocks.key: An ELISA standard curve is just a binding curve. It's most **sensitive at concentrations below or around the Kd**. Past the Kd it flattens out (saturates), so you need huge concentration changes to see any signal change. That's the end of the useful range.

blocks.p: Noise comes from **technical** variability (pipetting, plate, reader) and **biological** variability (real person-to-person or day-to-day differences).

example.q: COVID serology: everyone's antibodies have different variable regions. How can one test detect them all?
example.a: Put the COVID protein on the plate. Your antibodies bind it. Then a **secondary antibody against the human constant region** gives the signal. The constant region is the same for everyone.

videos.title: ELISA vs Western Blot (animated)
Sandwich ELISA explained, step by step

questions.question: In a western blot, what does the primary antibody provide?
questions.explanation: The primary binds the specific target. The labeled secondary provides sensitivity.

questions.question: In a western blot, what does the secondary antibody provide?
questions.explanation: The secondary recognizes the primary's constant region and carries the label, amplifying signal.

questions.question: What information does a western blot give that a standard ELISA does not?
questions.explanation: The western runs on SDS-PAGE first, so the band position shows size.

questions.question: Why is ELISA used instead of westerns for large numbers of samples?
options: It is plate-based and simpler to run in bulk
It is the only method that shows protein size
It needs no antibodies to detect the target
It separates proteins by density instead
questions.explanation: ELISA is optimized for many samples at once on a plate.

questions.question: In a sandwich ELISA, what happens to the signal as target concentration increases?
questions.explanation: The target bridges the capture and detection antibodies, so more target = more signal.

questions.question: In a competitive ELISA design, more target in the sample causes:
questions.explanation: The target blocks the labeled molecule from binding, so signal drops.

questions.question: On an ELISA standard curve, where is the assay most sensitive?
options: At concentrations below or near the Kd
Only at concentrations far above the Kd
Exactly at the top plateau of the curve
questions.explanation: The curve is steepest below ~Kd. Above that it saturates.

questions.question: What sets the upper end of an ELISA's useful range?
options: Binding sites saturating past the Kd
The size of the target on SDS-PAGE gels
The isoelectric point of the antibody
How many secondary antibodies are added
questions.explanation: Once binding saturates, big concentration changes barely change the signal.

questions.question: What is an epitope?
options: The part of a target an antibody binds
The constant region of any antibody
The label on the secondary antibody
The plastic plate surface in an ELISA
questions.explanation: The epitope is the specific region the antibody's binding pocket recognizes.

questions.question: How can a COVID serology test detect antibodies from any patient?
options: A secondary antibody recognizes the human constant region
Each patient's antibody gene gets sequenced before testing
Antibodies are purified and then weighed on an SDS gel
The test measures only the unique variable region itself
questions.explanation: The variable regions differ, but the constant region is shared, so a secondary against it gives the signal.

questions.question: Which are sources of noise in an immunoassay measurement? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Technical and biological variability both add noise. The epitope is just what's recognized.

questions.question: Which can ELISA be used to measure? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Class slide: proteins, lipids, and hormones can all be targets.
